3. Motivation of the simecol Package

Thomas Petzoldt

Source: vignettes/c-simecol-oop.qmd

1 Introduction: R as a Modeling Tool

Ecological modeling spans a wide spectrum of mathematical and computational paradigms—from simple differential equation systems to spatially explicit cellular automata and complex individual-based models (IBMs). Historically, ecological modeling workflows were often fragmented across multiple environments:

  1. Phase 1: Simulation models written in compiled languages (e.g., FORTRAN), paired with spreadsheet software (e.g., Excel) for data analysis and plotting.
  2. Phase 2: Simulation models implemented in general-purpose languages (e.g., Java or C++), using R solely for statistical analysis and visualization.
  3. Phase 3: End-to-end workflows—data processing, simulation modeling, and visualization—conducted directly within R.
  4. Phase 4: Hybrid, reproducible architectures where R serves as the high-level modeling, visualization, and user-interface layer, optionally delegating performance-critical routines to compiled C/C++ code, connecting to SQL databases, and embedding documentation via literate programming (historically Sweave, now Quarto/R Markdown).

1.1 Why R?

Originally developed as an open-source dialect of the S language (created at AT&T Bell Laboratories by John Chambers) by Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman, R has become a standard environment for computational statistics and scientific computing. Its key strengths for ecological modeling include:

  • A matrix- and vector-oriented programming paradigm suited for numerical operations.
  • A comprehensive, publication-quality graphics system.
  • Seamless extensibility via R packages as well as compiled C, C++, and Fortran routines.
  • Built-in documentation systems and literate programming tools for reproducible research.

1.2 The Pitfalls of Ad-Hoc Scripting

Despite its strengths, writing ecological models in R without a unifying structure often leads to familiar software engineering problems (“When all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail”):

  • Fragmented coding styles: Three modelers can easily produce seven incompatible script structures.
  • Lack of documentation: When research deadlines press, model structure and assumptions remain buried in ad-hoc scripts.
  • Copy-and-paste proliferation: Exploring new scenarios often results in duplicating entire script files. Introducing a single new parameter may require hacking multiple sections of code, and reading someone else’s script frequently feels harder than rewriting it from scratch.

2 Design Philosophy of simecol

The simecol package (simulation of ecological systems) addresses these challenges by providing a lightweight, object-oriented framework for implementing, sharing, and simulating ecological models in R.

2.1 Prototypes and Family Resemblance

Inspired by Ludwig Wittgenstein’s concepts of family resemblance (Familienähnlichkeit) and prototype-based thinking, simecol avoids rigid, overly prescriptive class hierarchies. Instead of forcing every ecological model into a single universal mold, it identifies the structural commonalities shared across diverse model families:

  • Tight coupling between algorithms and data: A model consists of both functional equations and the data structures they operate on.
  • Distinct categories of model data:
    • parms: Model parameters (constants).
    • init: Initial values of state variables.
    • inputs: External forcing data or time-dependent input variables.
    • times: Simulation time steps (from, to, by).
  • Structured functional components:
    • main: The core model function (e.g., derivatives for ODEs or state transition rules for discrete-time models).
    • equations: An optional list of nested sub-models or helper functions.
    • solver: The numerical integration or iteration algorithm, alongside standardized methods for data management and visualization.

2.2 The simObj Architecture

In simecol, models are encapsulated as S4 objects inheriting from the base class simObj. This class bundles all data slots and functional slots into a single self-contained object:

Slot Type Description
main function Core model equations or transition rules
equations list Optional list of sub-models or helper functions
times numeric Vector of simulation time steps
init ANY Initial state values (e.g., numeric vector, matrix, or data frame)
parms ANY Model parameters (e.g., numeric vector or list)
inputs ANY External time-series inputs or forcing functions
solver character Name of the solver function (e.g., "lsoda", "rk4", "euler", "iteration")
out ANY Simulation output stored after running sim()
initfunc function Optional initialization function executed when the object is created or modified

To accommodate different mathematical formulations, simecol provides specialized subclasses of simObj:

  • odeModel: Ordinary differential equation models (solved via wrappers to deSolve integrators such as lsoda, rk4, or euler).
  • gridModel: Spatially explicit, grid-based cellular automata (typically solved via discrete "iteration").
  • rwalkModel: Individual-based or random-walk models.
  • User-defined subclasses: Custom model families extending simObj.

Generic functions such as sim(), plot(), and print(), together with accessor functions (parms(), init(), times(), inputs(), equations(), solver(), and out()), provide a uniform user interface across all model types.

3 Core Examples

3.1 Example 1: Lotka-Volterra Predator-Prey Model (odeModel)

The classical Lotka-Volterra model describes the continuous-time dynamics of a prey population (X1X_1) and a predator population (X2X_2):

dX1dt=b⋅X1−e⋅X1⋅X2dX2dt=−d⋅X2+e⋅X1⋅X2\begin{aligned} \frac{dX_1}{dt} &= b \cdot X_1 - e \cdot X_1 \cdot X_2 \\ \frac{dX_2}{dt} &= -d \cdot X_2 + e \cdot X_1 \cdot X_2 \end{aligned}

In simecol, this system is defined as an odeModel object:

library("simecol")
lv <- new("odeModel",
  main = function(time, init, parms) {
    x <- init
    with(as.list(parms), {
      dx1 <-  b * x[1] - e * x[1] * x[2]
      dx2 <- -d * x[2] + e * x[1] * x[2]
      list(c(dx1, dx2))
    })
  },
  ##       birth,  encounter,  death
  parms  = c(b = 0.2, e = 0.2, d = 0.2),
  times  = seq(0, 100, 1),
  init   = c(prey = 0.5, predator = 1),
  solver = "lsoda" # solver function from the deSolve package
)

lv <- sim(lv)
plot(lv)

3.2 Example 2: Conway’s Game of Life (gridModel)

Cellular automata operate on discrete spatial grids updated over discrete time steps. In Conway’s Game of Life, each cell’s state X∈{0,1}X \in \{0, 1\} depends on the number of active neighbors NN in its 8-cell Moore neighborhood:

  • If X=1X = 1 and N∈{2,3}N \in \{2, 3\}, the cell survives (X:=1X := 1).
  • If X=0X = 0 and N=3N = 3, a new cell is born (X:=1X := 1).
  • Otherwise, the cell dies or remains empty (X:=0X := 0).

Using gridModel and the built-in eightneighbours() utility function, the model is written concisely in matrix form:

set.seed(123)
conway <- new("gridModel",
  main = function(time, init, parms) {
    x      <- init
    nb     <- eightneighbours(x)
    surviv <- (x >  0 & (nb %in% parms$srv))
    gener  <- (x == 0 & (nb %in% parms$gen))
    x      <- as.numeric((surviv + gener) > 0)
    dim(x) <- dim(init)
    return(x)
  },
  parms  = list(srv = c(2, 3), gen = 3),
  times  = 1:20,
  init   = matrix(round(runif(1000)), ncol = 40),
  solver = "iteration"
)

To run an animated simulation in an interactive R session, use animate = TRUE:

sim(conway, animate = TRUE, axes = FALSE)

4 Cloning and Modifying Models

A central workflow in simecol is cloning and modification—a hallmark of prototype-based object-oriented programming. Rather than copying and editing source files to test alternative hypotheses or parameter sets, users copy an existing simObj in memory and modify specific slots via accessor functions (init<-, parms<-, times<-, equations<-).

The following example clones the conway prototype, initializes a glider-like pattern on a 20×2020 \times 20 grid (life1), and then creates a second clone (life2) with modified survival and birth rules:

# Clone the prototype and set a custom initial grid
life1 <- conway
z <- matrix(0, 20, 20)
z[14, 10:12] <- z[13, 11] <- z[15, 12] <- 1
init(life1) <- z

# Clone life1 to create a second scenario with modified rules
life2 <- life1
parms(life2) <- list(srv = c(3, 4), gen = c(3, 4))

# Simulate both instances independently in memory
life1 <- sim(life1)
life2 <- sim(life2)
# Compare results
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(life1, index=20, main = "1) Standard Rules")
plot(life2, index=20, main = "2) Modified Rules")

Because life1 and life2 are independent S4 objects in memory, scenario comparisons remain clean, reproducible, and free of file duplication.

5 Individual-Based Models (IBMs) in R

A frequent question in ecological modeling is whether R’s high-level data structures can efficiently support individual-based models (IBMs).

5.1 Vectorized, Table-Oriented Design

While nested loops over thousands of individual objects can be slow in interpreted languages, R achieves strong performance when individuals are represented in tabular structures (data.frame or matrix) and updated in bulk using vectorized operations (“quasi-parallel” processing):

  • State updates (growth/aging): Vectorized column arithmetic updates all individuals simultaneously:

    inds$age    <- inds$age + delta_t
inds$weight <- inds$weight + assi(food, inds$weight, temp) * delta_t

  • Reproduction: Newly generated offspring are stored in a newinds table and appended via rbind(inds, newinds).

  • Mortality: Stochastic survival is evaluated across all rows at once using runif() and subset():

    survive <- function(inds, pmort = 0.01) {
  p <- runif(nrow(inds))
  subset(inds, p < pmort)
}

When performance bottlenecks still arise in complex spatial interactions, critical inner loops can be compiled in C or C++ and called directly from R.

5.2 Built-in IBM and Chaotic System Examples

The simecol package ships with ready-to-run example models illustrating both individual-based and multi-species chaotic dynamics, such as the chaotic Lotka-Volterra (UPCA) model:

data(upca)
out_upca <- out(sim(upca))
plot(out_upca, col = "navy")

6 Modular Sub-Equations

For larger ecological models, equations can be decomposed into modular, nested helper functions inside the equations slot. Functions listed in equations are automatically visible inside main, allowing users to inspect or replace individual sub-processes without rewriting the entire model:

logistic_model <- new("odeModel",
  main = function(time, init, parms) {
    x <- init
    dx1 <- f2(x[1], r = 0.1, K = 10)
    list(c(dx1))
  },
  equations = list(
    f1 = function(x, K)    K - x,
    f2 = function(x, r, K) r * x * f1(x, K)
  ),
  times = seq(0, 10, 0.1),
  init  = c(x = 0.5),
  solver = "lsoda"
)

plot(sim(logistic_model))

7 Summary

Combining prototype-inspired object orientation with R’s vectorized data structures makes ecological modeling both expressive and maintainable:

  • Clarity and reusability: Models are self-contained simObj instances that can be cloned, modified, and shared without copy-and-paste file proliferation.
  • Compact, vectorized code: Matrix and table-based representations allow cellular automata and individual-based models to be expressed concisely.
  • From users to developers: Because simecol models expose a consistent interface (sim(), plot(), parms(), init()), domain scientists can start by running existing models and gradually transition into modifying equations and developing their own model families.
